title: request-throttle-guardrails-and-eviction-playbook
body:
Purpose:
This is a practical design + playbook for throttling, admission control, and eviction behavior in the serving runtime. Focus: how scheduler-level decisions (queues / timeouts / per-tenant limits) interact with kernel selection and the KV cache to keep latency SLOs intact while maximizing throughput and fairness across tenants.

Context / motivation:
- We run a multi-tenant inference runtime that must balance latency SLOs (tail p99/p99.9), cost efficiency (high GPU utilization), and tenant fairness (no single tenant can starve others).
- Current problems observed in staging: long tail latencies when bursty tenants fill GPU slots, increased kernel context-switching when many short sequences are admitted concurrently, and KV cache thrash from multi-tenant working-set churn.
- Need a cohesive set of admission rules and eviction heuristics that are easy to reason about and operable by SREs.

Goals (non-exhaustive):
- Contain latency tail growth under bursty traffic.
- Provide predictable per-tenant request throughput under constrained capacity.
- Avoid unnecessary kernel switching/overheads by favoring batching-friendly admissions.
- Integrate KV cache awareness to avoid admitting requests that will immediately thrash hot KV shards.
- Make behavior observable and tunable via runtime knobs and metrics.

Assumptions:
- Each GPU instance exposes N execution slots (logical), but actual scheduling is continuous (we use batching/kernels).
- We can measure request-level signals: tenant_id, request_length_tokens, realtime_estimated_latency (model + kernel), affinity (cache hit probability), and priority_class (free/paid/enterprise).
- KV cache provides per-tenant hit-rate estimates and approximate working-set size telemetry.

High-level design summary:
1) Multi-level admission: per-tenant soft token bucket -> global fairness gate -> slot allocator with queue aging.
2) Soft vs hard timeouts: soft timeout triggers preemption/fallback while hard timeout terminates request and returns error/fallback model.
3) KV-aware scoring: requests are scored with a cache-impact factor; high-impact requests are deprioritized when cache pressure is high.
4) Kernel affinity hints: scheduler prefers to admit batches that align on kernel selection (same sequence length bucket / quantization) to reduce context switches.
5) Observability: per-tenant admitted rate, dropped/admitted counts, queue-age distribution, cache-hit delta after admission window.

Components and responsibilities:
- Admission Controller (AC): enforces per-tenant token buckets, tenant concurrency limits, and priority buckets. Emits admit/queue/reject decisions.
- Global Fairness Gate (GFG): ensures global capacity isn't overloaded by enforcing headroom for high-priority classes and preventing global saturation.
- Slot Allocator / Scheduler: selects which queued requests enter GPU execution; tries to maximize kernel affinity and batch size while respecting admitted set and timeouts.
- Eviction Manager: decides which queued or running requests to preempt if deadlines are missed or higher-priority tenant requires capacity. Communicates with model runtime to checkpoint KV cache state when relevant.
- KV Cache Monitor: emits cache-pressure signals: global miss-rate increase, per-tenant working-set churn, and hot-shard contention.

Admission flow (detailed):
1) Request arrives with metadata: (tenant T, len L, priority P, affinity A).
2) AC applies per-tenant token-bucket (rate R_T, burst B_T). If bucket empty -> "queue" unless queue over per-tenant queue limit Q_T -> then "reject" or "defer" depending on policy.
3) If token available, AC calculates score S = f(L, P, A, cache_impact(T)). If S > threshold_for_slot_shortage -> queue (prefer preferential admission later).
4) Requests that survive AC are offered to GFG. GFG enforces global headroom H_P for priority class P (e.g., keep 10% of slots free for enterprise emergencies). If no headroom -> either queue or reject depending on tenant SLAs.
5) Slot allocator picks candidates from prioritized queues (priority -> queue_age -> kernel_affinity -> batch_packing).
6) Running requests can be preempted by Eviction Manager if hard constraints violated (see below).

Queueing policies and timeouts:
- Per-tenant queue length Q_T defaults: 50 for free, 200 for paid, 1000 for enterprise (example).
- Global queue cap per node to prevent memory blowup.
- Soft timeout T_soft: e.g., 400ms beyond expected execution start; on soft timeout we attempt one of: re-route to a warm fallback node, switch to a smaller-kernel model variant, or mark as "deprioritized" (metrics).
- Hard timeout T_hard: e.g., 2x T_expected or absolute 3s; on hard timeout respond with structured error + fallback suggestion.
- Queue aging boost: requests waiting longer than age A_boost are escalated with an admission score multiplier M_age (e.g., 1.5x per A_boost threshold) to prevent starvation.

Per-tenant limits and token buckets:
- Token bucket parameters stored in config service and periodically reconciled. Tokens represent admission "credits" where cost_per_request = base_cost(L) * cache_penalty(T). base_cost(L) maps sequence length to token cost (short=1, medium=2, long=5).
- Example: Paid tenant R=100 tokens/sec, B=500. Immediately heavy burst reduces available tokens causing queuing.
- Concurrency caps: soft_concurrency (S_T) and hard_concurrency (H_T). If soft exceeded, new requests are queued; if hard exceeded, reject unless enterprise override.

KV cache integration (key part):
- Cache pressure heuristic: per-tenant cache_miss_rate trend over sliding window W (default 60s). If miss_rate_delta > X, mark tenant as "cache-thrashing".
- For thrashing tenants: increase cost_per_request by KV_penalty factor (e.g., x3) and temporarily shrink B_T to reduce admission. Also increase their eviction score for running requests.
- Admission uses cache-affinity hint: requests likely to hit the KV cache (cold-start false) get priority since they reduce aggregate work. We compute affinity A in 0..1.
- When admitting a request with expected high cache write pressure (e.g., new context updates), Eviction Manager will avoid admitting many such writes simultaneously if they would evict the same hot shard. Instead we serialize those admissions with small windows to amortize eviction cost.

Kernel affinity and batching optimization:
- Kernel selection is expensive when switching between quantization/sequence-length-specialized kernels. We add a kernel-affinity score to admission scoring so scheduler groups requests by kernel class.
- For short sequences: encourage burst admission until a small batch threshold B_min (e.g., 8 tokens/batch) to utilize GPU. For long sequences: prefer immediate admission if tokens_remaining will underutilize kernel long-tail otherwise.
- Scheduler tries packable cohorts: rule-of-thumb is to prefer same model variant and same seq-length bucket within each dispatch cycle.

Eviction and preemption rules:
- Preemption prioritized: lowest effective priority (priority_class * (1 - age_boost) * (1 + cache_penalty)) -> candidate for preemption.
- Preemption actions: gracefully pause KV updates (if supported), dump partial KV state to ephemeral cache, requeue request to another node or return fallback response.
- Prefer to preempt queued requests over running requests. Running requests only preempted for SLA-critical events or persistent deadline miss.

Operational signals and SLOs to monitor:
- Per-node: admitted_rate, rejected_rate, avg_queue_latency, p95_queue_latency, p99_queue_latency, kernel_switch_rate, batch_utilization, gpu_taking_time.
- Per-tenant: admitted_tokens/sec, queue_length, cache_miss_rate, avg_start_delay, request_rejects.
- Alerts: sustained p99_queue_latency > X, kernel_switch_rate jump > 3x baseline, cache_miss_rate_delta > 0.2 for > 60s.

Tuning knobs (runtime config):
- global_headroom_by_priority: map priority->percentage of slots held in reserve.
- per_tenant_token_profile: R/B values, soft/hard concurrency, reject_policy.
- kernel_affinity_weight: weight applied to affinity in scoring (0..1).
- cache_penalty_thresholds: miss_rate_delta thresholds and penalty multipliers.
- age_boost_params: thresholds and multipliers.

Integration tests and experiments (recommended):
1) Synthetic burst test: 100 tenants, one 10x burst tenant -> measure p99 for others with/without KV-aware penalties.
2) Kernel-switching test: mixed seq length distribution with high churn, measure kernel_switch_rate and tail latency.
3) Cache-churn test: two tenants share hot shards; simulate writes and observe eviction and admission.
4) Headroom policy test: set headroom low vs high and observe emergency tenant admission behavior.

Operational playbook (for SRE/Oncall):
- If p99 queue latency spikes: check kernel_switch_rate and per-tenant admission rates. If kernel_switch high -> reduce kernel_affinity_weight to force stricter grouping.
- If a tenant is thrashing cache -> limit its burst token bucket and evict long-running low-priority requests; consider a temporary targeted throttle and notify tenant.
- If global saturation persists -> increase global_headroom for enterprise and escalate to capacity planning.

Sample pseudo-code (admission scoring):
- Note: intentionally simple to be implemented in AC component.

function score_request(req, tenant_state, node_state):
  base = length_cost(req.length)
  pr = priority_weight(req.priority)  // higher for enterprise
  age = 1 + age_boost(req.wait_time)
  cache_pen = 1 + cache_penalty_factor(tenant_state.cache_miss_delta)
  kernel_aff = kernel_affinity_score(req, node_state.recent_kernel)
  score = (pr * age * kernel_aff) / (base * cache_pen)
  return score

Admission decision: if token_bucket.has(req.cost) and node_state.available_slots > low_watermark and score >= admission_threshold then admit else queue_or_reject

Open questions / tradeoffs (list):
- Should we allow tokens to be bought-back by enterprise tenants momentarily if they pay for burst credits? (billing complexity)
- How aggressive should KV penalties be before they reduce tenant throughput too much and impact UX? We need to quantify with real workloads.
- How to best checkpoint or migrate KV partial state on preemption without losing correctness?

Rollout plan (safe):
- Phase 1: Implement admission controller and token buckets as a configuration-only path (no enforced penalties) and collect metrics for 2 weeks.
- Phase 2: Enable queueing + soft timeouts in non-prod and run synthetic tests.
- Phase 3: Gradually enable KV-penalty enforcement at 10% of nodes, monitor per-tenant latency/throughput.
- Phase 4: Global rollout with per-tenant override flags for support teams.

TODOs:
- Implement per-tenant token cost formula in config service (INF-1427).
- Add a kernel-affinity metric to trace payloads (PR #789).
- Write confluence doc with operator runbook and playbook snippets.

References and links:
- GitHub: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/789 (kernel-affinity work)
- Jira: JIRA-INF-1427 (token-cost refactor)
- Design notes: confluence://designs/scheduler-v2

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep interaction model simple: cache penalties should slow admission, not cause immediate hard rejects. We want gradual backoff so UX for paying tenants is predictable.
- Watch for complexity blowup: too many knobs -> operators ignore them. Start with 4–5 strong signals: token_rate, soft_concurrency, cache_miss_delta, kernel_affinity.

End of draft.
